The German noun 'Autotür' is feminine..why: The compound is uncommon ('Autotür' 115 hits, 'die Autotür' 16) and its gender is almost never stated, while 'Tür' and its gender are everywhere. A model most likely gets the gender of 'Autotür' from its last element. Rated likely, not very likely: Wiktionary's entry does give the gender.

sources.note: One of the few places the gender is stated.
The direct forms are rare; the head and its article are frequent.

The German noun 'Tür' is feminine..why: 'die Tür' is basic German vocabulary; Wiktionary gives the gender.

'Autotür' takes the gender of its last e.why: The word is visibly 'Auto' + 'Tür', and German compounds take the gender of their last element. The rule has lexicalised exceptions (die Demut beside der Mut), which is why this premise, for one word, is the one that gives way.

sources.quote: Compound words usually carry the gender of their last element.

A German compound noun that takes the ge.why: Definitional, like 'a building observes the time zone of the city it stands in': taking the gender of the last element just means having that element's gender. It never gives way; whether this word takes its last element's gender is the second premise.

notes: Mirrors grammar-replace-0015: removes 'Autotür is feminine'. Every derived query goes through the deleted gender and expects 'does not know'; Q1 is the premise route through the premises' description, where a model answering 'die' has hidden the conclusion and re-derived it.
